subject: chemistry_2
question_text: How many moles of AgCl are precipitated when 1 mole of CoCl₃ is treated with AgNO₃?

verification.note: Unit 11 (d and f Block Elements) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", printed chapter 8 ("8. d & f BLOCK ELEMENTS"), book pp.91-94, which prints this question on book p.92 as VSAQ 11. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. BOOK TYPO (book p.92, VSAQ 11): the question is printed as "1 mole of COCl₃", with a capital O. CO is carbon monoxide and Co is cobalt; the compound meant is cobalt(III) chloride, CoCl₃, which is how the book's own answer line writes it. The question text on this card is corrected to CoCl₃ and the typo is recorded here. ANSWER CHECKED: three ionisable chloride ions give three moles of AgCl, and the book's equation CoCl₃ + 3AgNO₃ → 3AgCl + Co(NO₃)₃ is balanced. CONTEXT ADDED: the same count of 3 comes from [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃, where all three chloride ions lie outside the coordination sphere; the count falls to 2 for [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂ and to 1 for [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]Cl. That series is what the question is really testing, and it links to Werner's primary and secondary valency in Short Answer 1 of the same chapter.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question
d and f Block Elements — 2 marks

steps.label: The equation
lines: All three chloride ions in CoCl₃ are
One mole of ionisable chloride gives one
steps.why: Silver nitrate precipitates only the chloride that is free in solution, so counting moles of AgCl is the same as counting ionisable chloride. In CoCl₃ every chloride is outside the coordination sphere, the ratio is one to one, and three moles are precipitated. The book prints the formula in the question as COCl₃; Co is cobalt and CO is carbon monoxide, so that is a printing slip.
common_mistakes: Balancing with one AgNO₃. Three chloride ions need three silver ions.
Leaving out the precipitate. AgCl is the white solid, and it is what the question is counting.
steps.memory_tip: One free chloride gives one AgCl. Count the chloride written outside the square bracket.
steps.margin_note: The balanced equation is worth as much as the number. Write it before the answer.

steps.label: The answer
lines: where all three chloride ions lie outside
The count changes when chloride moves
steps.why: Werner used exactly this test to build his theory. Chloride inside the coordination sphere is held by a secondary valency, is not ionisable and is not precipitated; chloride outside is held by a primary valency, is ionisable and is precipitated. Reading the count straight off the formula is what the question is testing, so the series 3, 2, 1 is worth writing.
common_mistakes: Counting every chloride in the formula. Only the chloride outside the square bracket is precipitated.
Writing 3 with no unit. The answer is 3 moles of AgCl.
steps.memory_tip: Chloride outside the bracket is precipitated; chloride inside is not.
steps.margin_note: The number alone is half. Add one line naming which chloride is precipitated and why.

insider_note: The examiner is testing primary and secondary valency, not arithmetic. Use the phrase "ionisable chloride" somewhere in the answer.
